params.why: the union cannot have more outcomes than the sample space

stem: In a probability experiment the sample space $S$ has $n(S)={=nS}$ equally likely outcomes. For two events $A$ and $B$ it is known that $n(A)={=nA}$, $n(B)={=nB}$ and $n(A\cup B)={=nU}$. Calculate the value of $P(A\cap B)$. Give your answer as a decimal number.
solution: The probability of a union is $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.
Make $P(A\cap B)$ the subject, and we get: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cup B)$.
The probability of an event $X$ is $P(X)=\frac{n(X)}{n(S)}$, and here $n(S)={=nS}$.
Therefore, the value of $P(A\cap B)$ is ${=ans}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Adds P(A) and P(B) and stops
proposed_misconceptions.description: Gives P(A) + P(B) as the answer and never subtracts P(A∪B), so the overlap is not isolated; the formula P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) is not rearranged.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Divides by n(A∪B) instead of n(S)
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses the size of the union as the denominator when turning counts into probabilities, instead of the size of the whole sample space.

notes: Entry-point skill: the book's own rearrangement P(A∩B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∪B) (parent ex14-8-24), with the counts n(A), n(B), n(A∪B), n(S) given directly so the learner does not also have to read the event-set tables. n(S) is drawn from 20, 25, 50, 100 so every probability and the answer is an exact two-decimal number: no rounded-intermediate disagreement (the book's own 0.33 + 0.5 - 0.67 = 0.16 versus its stated 0.17 is exactly that trap). n(A) and n(B) are 3 to 10, the overlap is at least 1 and strictly smaller than both sets, so neither event sits inside the other and n(A∪B) ≤ 19 ≤ n(S). The key prints as two decimals (e.g. 0.40); the stem says only 'decimal number'. Checked by brute force over all 1072 parameter combinations: pA + pB - pU equals nI/nS exactly in every one.
